title: God in the dust of the road
hook: a poet tells a worshiper to open the temple doors and look outside
carry: seva: god is with the ones who work

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tagore's Gitanjali opened with a reed flute: bhakti, where we offer God what God gave first.

A dark corner of a temple. The doors are shut. Someone sits there with a string of beads, chanting, eyes closed. It's a real and honored form of devotion. And in one Gitanjali poem, the poet walks up to that person and says, in effect: stop. Open your eyes. Your God isn't before you. Today, poem eleven, and where Tagore says to look instead.
screen: `A DARK CORNER, DOORS SHUT.` → `OPEN YOUR EYES.` → `WHERE TO LOOK INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines, in Tagore's own English: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!" Then he says where God is: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones." God is with them in sun and in shower, the poem says, his garment covered in dust, and it tells the worshiper to put off the holy mantle and come down onto the dusty soil too. Tagore's family belonged to the Brahmo Samaj, a reform movement wary of image worship, and the poem carries that voice. Hindus who pray with beads and flowers may answer that their worship is where they learn to see God in the field. But both stand on one old teaching. In the Gita, Krishna says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. If that's true, God isn't only behind the shut doors. The poem even asks where deliverance could be found, since the master himself has joyfully taken on the bonds of creation. Hindus have a word for worship done with the hands: seva, service. Temple kitchens run on it, volunteers chopping and stirring so anyone who walks in can eat, and many families count that hour as worship, not time away from it. The poem closes: meet him and stand by him in toil and in the sweat of thy brow. The place of worship and the place of work turn out to be the same place.
screen: `LEAVE THE CHANTING, OPEN YOUR EYES.` · `GOD IS WITH THE TILLER AND THE PATHMAKER.` · `THE LORD DWELLS IN EVERY HEART.` · `SEVA: WORSHIP WITH THE HANDS.` · then, large: `MEET HIM IN TOIL.`

segments.voice: Open your eyes and let your gaze rest on what's in front of you. Bring to mind someone whose work you depend on and rarely see, whoever grew today's food, laid the road outside or cleans the building, and stay with one of them, at work in sun or rain. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, right where they're working; if not, simply keep them in view, with some gratitude.
Tagore's Gitanjali. In poem eleven, the doors come open, and God is found where the tiller tills and the pathmaker breaks stones.
Your line: seva: God is with the ones who work. Tomorrow, a raised palm that says fear not. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Many Hindu temples run kitchens where volunteers cook and serve whoever comes, and many families count this seva as worship alongside prayer with beads, flowers and incense.
